documents.title: Efficacy and safety of gut microbiome-targeted treatment in patients with depression: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The study aimed to comprehensively analyze and establish a framework for evaluating the efficacy of microbiome-targeted treatment (MTT) for depression.
METHODS: We searched PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, and the Chinese National Knowledge Infrastructure database for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) on MTT in treating depression until October 19, 2023. A meta-analysis was conducted to evaluate the efficacy and safety of MTT. Comprehensive subgroup analyses were undertaken to explore factors influencing MTT's efficacy in treating depression. This study was registered with PROSPERO (CRD42023483649).
RESULTS: The study selection process identified 51,570 studies, of which 34 met the inclusion criteria. The overall pooled estimates showed that MTT significantly improved depression symptoms (SMD -0.26, 95% CI [-0.32, -0.19], I2 = 54%) with acceptable safety. Subgroup analyses by geography showed that effectiveness was demonstrated in Asia (SMD -0.46, 95% CI [-0.56, -0.36], I2 = 36%), while no evidence of effectiveness was found in Europe (SMD -0.07, 95% CI [-0.19, 0.05], I2 = 55%), America (SMD -0.33, 95% CI [-0.67, 0.02], I2 = 60%), and Oceania (SMD 0.00, 95% CI [-0.18, 0.18], I2 = 0%). Besides, the efficacy was shown in depressed patients without comorbidities (SMD -0.31, 95% CI [-0.40, -0.22], I2 = 0%), whereas effectiveness was poor in those with digestive disorders, such as irritable bowel syndrome (SMD -0.37, 95% CI [-0.89, 0.16], I2 = 74%), chronic diarrhea (SMD -0.34, 95% CI [-0.73, 0.05]), and chronic constipation (SMD -0.23, 95% CI [-0.57, 0.11], I2 = 0%). In perinatal depressed patients, MTT was not effective (SMD 0.16, 95% CI [0.01, 0.31], I2 = 0%). It was found that 2 = 0%) and 8-12 weeks (SMD -0.34, 95% CI [-0.44, -0.23], I2 = 57%) MTT were effective, while > 12 weeks (SMD 0.02, 95% CI [-0.12, 0.17], I2 = 68%) MTT was ineffective.
CONCLUSIONS: Despite the overall effectiveness of MTT in treating depression and its acceptable safety profile, caution is warranted in drawing this conclusion due to limitations posed by the small sample size of included studies and heterogeneity. The efficacy of MTT for depression exhibits variation influenced by geography, patient comorbidities, and duration of administration.

Background Depression is the leading cause of global mental health-related impairments and represents a substantial international mental health challenge [ 1 ]. It is widespread, costly, incapacitating, and associated with an increased risk of suicide. Depression has a functional impact on individuals of all ages. However, it may be especially severe in adults over the age of 18, where co-existing physical health conditions can exacerbate its effects and complicate treatment options [ 2 ]. While antidepressants may be effective, their therapeutic effects typically take up to six weeks to manifest and are often associated with common side effects [ 3 ]. Additionally, multiple medications are frequently necessary to alleviate depressive symptoms. Notably, 30–50% of patients with major depressive disorder (MDD) exhibit only partial responses to multiple antidepressants [ 4 ]. Furthermore, in individuals with ineffective initial treatments, even if subsequent treatments are effective, there is a very high relapse rate while continuing the treatment [ 5 ]. Although guidelines from the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, for example, recommend a comprehensive psychosocial intervention for depression treatment, its efficacy for patients with moderate or severe depression is still debatable [ 6 ]. Therefore, there is an urgent need for the development of new treatments for depression. Microbiome-targeted therapy (MTT) is a proposed approach for modulating the gut microbiome. It can be categorized into probiotics, synbiotics, antibiotics, and fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) [ 7 ]. An increasing number of studies indicated a potential correlation between gut microbiota dysbiosis and depression [ 8 , 9 ]. The gut microbiota composition is altered in patients diagnosed with MDD compared to healthy individuals. These changes are associated with the relative abundance and diversity of specific bacterial taxa [ 10 ]. MTT is considered a potential treatment for depression due to its ability to maneuver gut microbes and regulate their metabolisms. However, to date, there is still a lack of comprehensive research on the factors influencing the efficacy of MTT in treating depression, resulting in significant heterogeneity across current studies. The impact of various confounding factors should not be overlooked when analyzing changes in microbial structure and function in depression [ 11 ]. Furthermore, it is important to emphasize that differences in efficacy from depression involve the variability in different geographical regions, patients’ comorbidities, and administration durations in different studies. Given that the differences in the efficacy of MTT for depression remain unclear with respect to these factors, further exploration of the underlying connections is warranted. This study performed a meta-analysis evaluating the efficacy and safety of MTT for depression, considering geographical region, administration duration and patient comorbidity, thereby providing a foundation for the clinical application of MTT. Methods This meta-analysis was designed and conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses (PRISMA) reporting guideline (Appendix 1 of Supplementary material 1 ) [ 12 ]. The present protocol has been registered within the PROSPERO database (registration number: CRD42023483649). Design and search strategy The search included articles published in the PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, and Chinese National Knowledge Infrastructure database through October, 19, 2023. We identified the search strategy by combining terms indicative of MTT (probiotics, prebiotics, synbiotics, fecal microbiota transplantation) and depression (both MeSH-terms and text words). The detailed retrieval strategy can be found in the Supplementary material 1 (see Appendix 2 for the full electronic search strategy). Criteria for inclusion and exclusion Two authors independently reviewed the title and abstract of each identified article and then cross-checked. Inclusion criteria were based on the following PICO(S) (Participants/Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome, Study Design) principles: Participants/Population: All subjects had a diagnosis of depression or a risk of developing depression. Intervention MTT applications, including probiotics, prebiotics, and synbiotics. Comparator: a placebo or with no intervention. Outcome(s): (1) Main outcome: efficacy measure, change in depression scale scores from the baseline to the end of follow-up period, including but not limited to the following depression scales: Beck’s Depression Inventory (BDI), Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS), the Depression Anxiety and Stress Scales (DASS), Hamilton Depression Scale (HAM-D), Hamilton Depression Rating scale (HDRS), Montgomery and Asberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS). (2) Additional outcomes: biochemical assay including the Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), the C-reactive protein (CRP), the cortisol, and the cytokines levels; adverse events (including but not limited to abdominal upset, bloating, nausea, diarrhea, constipation, flatulence, fever, etc.) Study design: All RCTs with or without blinding. Studies were excluded if (1) study reported insufficient details to derive the study outcomes; (2) the full text of the study was not available in the databases; (3) study was on an animal model. Data extraction Two investigators performed the literature search and screening, and two investigators independently performed data extraction. If only figures were presented, the two investigators independently used Get Data Graph Digitizer ver. 2.26 to extract data and compute the means [ 13 ]. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion between investigators. The extracted data items include (1) study design, country, year of publication; (2) participant characteristics, including size, female percentage, BMI, and comorbidities; (3) details of the intervention, treatment duration. An additional file shows this in more detail. The location of authors institute affiliations for all papers were classified into Asia, Europe, America, Oceania and Africa. Subgroup analysis To examine whether the observed effects of MTT on depression varied in terms of the moderator variables, the following subgroup analyses were conducted based on the presence of depression scales, administration duration, continents and demography, MTT types, percentage of females, presence of comorbidities, overweight or not, and pre- or post- COVID-19. Risk of bias We scored the studies that met inclusion criteria according to the Cochrane risk of bias tool [ 14 ], which evaluated the random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of participants, personal and outcome assessment, incomplete outcome data, selective outcome reporting, and other biases. The included RCTs were classified as low risk (L), high risk (H) or unclear risk (U) in the above items. Statistical analysis In the present study, the variables were pooled according to the different data types. For the continuous variables, the standardized mean difference (SMD) with 95% confidence intervals (95% CIs) was calculated when different scales were used between studies to measure the same outcome. In addition, the mean difference (MD) with 95% CIs was calculated when the same method was employed. For the dichotomous variables, the risk ratio with 95% CI was used. If the trial did not report a particular continuous outcome in the form of a mean and standard deviation, the values were converted for merging based on the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions version 6.4 [ 15 ] and Wang’s method [ 16 ]. We assessed heterogeneity using the I 2 value, which estimates the amount of total variation that is attributable to heterogeneity. If the values were < 50%, a fixed effects model was chosen. If heterogeneity was > 50%, we selected a random effects model and explored sources of heterogeneity using further subgroup analysis [ 17 ]. Sensitivity analysis was used to assess the robustness of the aggregated results. A two tailed α< 0.05 was considered to indicate statistical significance. Statistics were analyzed with RevMan 5.4 and Stata 15. Results Study selection and characteristics An initial Internet search yielded 51,570 potentially relevant studies. After eliminating duplicates, 49,864 studies remained. Of these studies titles and abstracts were reviewed, 49,718 studies were excluded. Of the remaining 96 studies, 62 were excluded after two reviewers independently reviewed the full text for the following reasons: ineligible interventions and outcomes, participants or interventions were not relevant, and studies were on an animal model. Finally, 34 studies [ 18 – 51 ] that compared MTT with placebo fulfilled all inclusion criteria (Supplementary material 1 : Appendix 3 ). Among the 34 studies included, there were several different types of MTT interventions and outcome measures in the same study, so 51 eligible trials were ultimately included in the meta-analysis. Of the 51 eligible trials, 27 originated from Asia, 14 from Europe, 3 from America, and 7 from Oceania (Fig. 1 ). Regarding comorbidities, 32 studies encompassed patients without comorbidities, 5 focused on pregnant patients, 4 examined patients with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), 3 explored those with coronary artery disease, 2 addressed chronic constipation, while individual studies evaluated patients with chronic diarrhea, inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), self-reported insomnia, and hemodialysis. Among the MTT types, probiotics were featured in 42 studies, prebiotics in 7 studies, and synbiotics in 3 studies. In addition, 20 studies had an administration duration of < 8 weeks, 24 spanned 8–12 weeks, and 7 extended beyond 12 weeks. The main characteristics of the included RCTs were described in the Table S1 of Supplementary material 2 . The details of MTT administration used were shown in the Table S2 of Supplementary material 2. Fig. 1 Global RCTs on MTT for depression Quality assessment Of the included trials, one study did not provide adequate details on allocation concealment. One study did not blind the psychiatrists, and three studies did not provide information on the blinding of participants and personnel. We assessed the study quality and risk of bias in accordance with specific conditions. The risk of bias assessment for individual studies and its summary is presented in Fig. 2 . Fig. 2 Assessment for risk of bias in included studies Depression scores The first part of our main meta-analysis investigated the different effects of MTT and placebo on depression scores. Altogether, 1662 patients receiving MTT and 1681 patients receiving controls were extracted from the 51 eligible trials. The antidepressant effect was better in the MTT group than in the control group. Compared with the placebo group, the MTT group showed positive effects on depression scale scores (SMD −0.26, 95% CI [−0.32, −0.19], I 2 = 54%). Forest plots of this analysis are presented in Fig. 3 . Fig. 3 The overall pooled estimates of MTT efficacy for depression Biochemical assay In the second part of the meta-analysis, we compared the biochemical assay between patients receiving MTT and those receiving control drugs. It was found that MTT significantly increased BDNF levels (SMD 0.19, 95% CI [0.02, 0.36], I 2 = 74%) (Fig. 4 a) compared to controls. In contrast, MTT treatment could significantly decrease CRP (SMD −0.55, 95% CI [−0.73, −0.37], I 2 = 86%) (Fig. 4 b) and cortisol (SMD −0.22, 95% CI [−0.43, −0.02], I 2 = 90%) (Fig. 4 f) levels. In terms of cytokines, MTT significantly reduced IL-6 (SMD −0.43, 95% CI [−0.64, −0.22], I 2 = 36%) (Fig. 4 c) levels but had no significant effect on IL-10 (SMD 0.13, 95% CI [−0.20,0.46], I 2 = 0%) (Fig. 4 d) and TNF-α (SMD −0.15, 95% CI [−0.33, 0.03], I 2 = 0%) levels (Fig. 4 e). Fig. 4 Forest plot of biochemical indices modulated by MTT in patients with depression Subgroup analysis Different depression scales Subgroup analysis for depression scores among different depression scales showed that MTT had beneficial effects on BDI (MD −1.37, 95% CI [−1.88, −0.86], I 2 = 35%), HAM-D (MD −1.60, 95% CI [−2.22, −0.99], I 2 = 2%), MADRS (MD −2.74, 95% CI [−4.52, −0.96], I 2 = 45%), HADS (MD −2.12, 95% CI [−2.64, −1.59], I 2 = 18%). However, no benefit was shown for MTT in terms of improved EPDS (MD 0.65, 95% CI [0.55, 1.25], I 2 = 0%) and DASS (MD −0.82, 95% CI [−8.54, 6.91], I 2 = 0%) compared to the placebo group (Supplementary material 1 : Appendix 4 ). Different administration duration Subgroup analysis based on different administration durations found that < 8 weeks (SMD −0.33, 95% CI [−0.45, −0.22], I 2 = 0%) and 8–12 weeks (SMD −0.34, 95% CI [−0.44, −0.23], I 2 = 57%) MTT were effective compared to the control group, while > 12 weeks MTT (SMD 0.02, 95% CI [−0.12, 0.17], I 2 = 68%) were found no effectiveness for depression (Fig. 5 ). Fig. 5 Subgroup analysis of different administration durations of MTT for depression Different continents and demography Given that the disease burden of depression and the gut microflora abundance differ across continents and ethnicities, which may affect the efficacy of MTT in the treatment of depression, we therefore performed a relevant subgroup analysis. The results showed that MTT for depression showed efficacy in Asia (SMD −0.46, 95% CI [−0.56, −0.36], I 2 = 36%), whereas no efficacy was shown in Europe (SMD −0.07, 95% CI [−0.19, 0.05], I 2 = 55%), America (SMD −0.33, 95% CI [−0.67, 0.02], I 2 = 60%) and Oceania (SMD 0.00, 95% CI [−0.18, 0.18], I 2 = 0%). Africa could not be analyzed due to the lack of studies and data (Fig. 6 ). Fig. 6 Subgroup analysis of different continents and demography Different MTT types Subgroup analysis according to the MTT types found that probiotic (SMD −0.22, 95% CI [−0.30, −0.15], I 2 = 47%), prebiotic (SMD −0.37, 95% CI [−0.61, −0.14], I 2 = 14%) and synbiotic (SMD −0.90, 95% CI [−1.26, −0.54], I 2 = 83%) all significantly improved depression scores. Fecal transplants were not analyzed due to the lack of published data (Supplementary material 1 : Appendix 5 ). Percentage of females Subgroup analysis based on the female percentage found that MTT significantly improved depression scores when the female percentage was< 80% (SMD −0.28, 95% CI [−0.37, −0.18], I 2 = 22%), while no efficacy was shown when it was ≥ 80% (SMD −0.08, 95% CI [−0.20, 0.03], I 2 = 60%) (Supplementary material 1 : Appendix 6 ). Presence of comorbidities or not Subgroup analysis found that MTT significantly reduced depression scores in patients without comorbidities (SMD −0.31, 95% CI [−0.40, −0.22], I 2 = 0%). The benefits were also found in patients with IBD (SMD −0.91, 95% CI [−1.53, −0.28]), coronary artery disease (SMD −0.67, 95% CI [−1.05, −0.29], I 2 = 19%), self-reported insomniacs (SMD −0.68, 95% CI [−1.32, −0.04]) and hemodialysis (SMD −1.37, 95% CI [−2.25, −0.49], I 2 = 75%). However, it was determined that MTT did not improve depression symptoms in pregnant patients (SMD 0.16, 95% CI [0.01, 0.31], I 2 = 0%). Additionally, no benefit of MTT for depression was shown in patients with IBS (SMD −0.37, 95% CI [−0.89, 0.16], I 2 = 74%), chronic constipation (SMD −0.23, 95% CI [−0.57, 0.11], I 2 = 0%), and chronic diarrhea (SMD −0.34, 95% CI [−0.73, 0.05]) (Fig. 7 ). Fig. 7 Subgroup analysis of the MTT efficacy for depressed patients with comorbidities or not Overweight or not According to the WHO standard for BMI classification of overweight, participants in this study were divided into BMI < 25 kg/m 2 (non-overweight group) and ≥ 25 kg/m 2 (overweight group) groups. It was found that MTT for depression was effective in both the non-overweight group (SMD −0.32, 95% CI [−0.43, −0.21], I 2 = 0%) and the overweight group (SMD −0.36, 95% CI [−0.45, −0.27], I 2 = 37%) (Supplementary material 1 : Appendix 7 ). Pre- or post-COVID-19 It was found that MTT for depression showed efficacy either before (SMD −0.44, 95% CI [−0.61, −0.26], I 2 = 42%) or after COVID-19 (SMD −0.27, 95% CI [−0.39, −0.14], I 2 = 56%) (Supplementary material 1 : Appendix 8 ). Adverse effects The effect of MTT on adverse reactions, including abdominal upset, bloating, nausea, diarrhea, constipation, flatulence, fever, and body ache, and increased appetite was investigated. The MTT group had a higher risk of abdominal upset (RR 2.27, 95% CI [1.16, 4.46], I 2 = 0%) (Fig. 8 a) and increased appetite (RR 6.64, 95% CI [1.53, 28.86], I 2 = 0%) (Fig. 8 b). However, MTT did not increase the risk of nausea (RR 1.63, 95% CI [0.90, 2.92], I 2 = 0%) (Fig. 8 c), diarrhea (RR 1.60, 95% CI [0.56, 4.54], I 2 = 0%) (Fig. 8 d), constipation (RR 1.55, 95% CI [0.56,4.34], I 2 = 0%) (Fig. 8 e), bloating (RR 1.55, 95% CI [0.56,4.34], I 2 = 0%) (Fig. 8 f), flayulence (RR 0.64, 95% CI [0.33,1.24], I 2 = 0%) (Fig. 8 g), and fever and body ache (RR 2.77, 95% CI [0.30,25.89], I 2 = 0%) (Fig. 8 h). Fig. 8 The effect of MTT treatment on adverse reactions Sensitivity analysis using a one-by-one elimination method, it was found that the combined outcome did not significantly change with each result removed from the included literature (Fig. 9 and Supplementary material 1 : Appendix 9 ), suggesting that the merged outcome was stable. Fig. 9 Results of sensitivity analysis using the one-by-one exclusion method. The numerical order corresponds to the order of study in Fig. 3 Discussion In this meta-analysis, MTT significantly improved depressive symptoms in patients and modulated biochemical indicators, including BDNF, CRP, cortisol, and IL-6. However, there was a high heterogeneity in the present study. A recent network meta-analysis found that probiotics may be effective as adjunctive or stand-alone therapies in the treatment of MDD compared to antidepressants and placebo. This was consistent with the findings of our study [ 52 ]. Another umbrella review of systematic reviews of randomized clinical trials assessed the efficacy and safety of probiotics for depression, however, due to the high heterogeneity of patients diagnosed with depression and anxiety, the results were limited in terms of the certainty of evidence [ 53 ]. In addition to the issue of heterogeneity, a meta-analysis noted that critical questions about species administered, dosage and timing relative to other antidepressant medications remained to be answered [ 54 ]. Individuals should be followed for longer periods of time before these therapies are implemented in clinical practice [ 55 ]. Since high heterogeneity and multiple confounding subgroup factors can hinder guideline development and reduce the precision of clinical decision-making, the present study was updated to include the latest RCTs and to explore the heterogeneity in terms of different geographical regions, patient characteristics (especially pregnant women), patient comorbidities, and administration durations, providing more comprehensive evidence on the efficacy of MTT for depression (Fig. 10 ). Fig. 10 The graphical overview of MTT efficacy in treating depression. Created on BioRender.com The burden of depression varies by geographic region and demographic factors, highlighting the need to understand regional differences when setting global health objectives. It was found that MTT was effective for depression in Asia, while the efficacy in Europe, America, and Oceania was still debatable in the present study. This may be attributed to the fewer studies from Europe, the Americas, and Oceania that were included, leaving the efficacy of MTT for depression to be inadequately represented from these regions in the present study. In addition, another reason may be individual variation in the gut microbiome across different regions and demographic groups. It was demonstrated that demographic factors represent the largest source of individual variation in the gut microbiome, especially dietary structure. Asian diets are typically higher in carbohydrates and lower in fats, which may increase beneficial bacteria (e.g., Firmicutes and Lactobacillus) and reduce non-beneficial bacteria (e.g., Bacteroidetes) [ 56 ]. In contrast, Western diets, characterized by higher fat and lower fiber content, have been associated with increased abundance of non-beneficial bacterial and decreased levels of beneficial bacterial. In depression, Firmicutes, Actinobacteria, and Bacteroidetes are the most affected phyla, with a notable increase in the Bacteroidetes/Firmicutes ratio in MDD patients [ 10 ]. Notably, dysbiosis in depressed patients is characterized by a decrease in beneficial bacteria and an increase in non-beneficial bacteria, and this change seems to coincide with the long-term gut flora characteristics in populations resulting from Western dietary patterns. These explain the geographic and demographic variation in MTT for depression. Different patient characteristics are associated with the complexity of depressive symptoms, especially in depressed pregnant women. Depressive symptoms are common during pregnancy and are estimated to affect 7–20% of pregnant women, even impacting their offspring health [ 57 ]. The onset of perinatal depression is associated with changes in reproductive hormones, stress hormones, and neurosteroids, which can be modulated by the gut microbiota, affecting maternal mental health during the perinatal period via the gut-brain-axis [ 58 ]. Nevertheless, it was surprising that no benefit and even potential detriment was associated with MTT for patients with depression in pregnancy in this study. In a RCT involving 380 women, taking a probiotic from weeks 14–16 of pregnancy until 6 months postpartum resulted in significantly lower depression and anxiety scores [ 59 ]. Yet, the study was funded by the supplement manufacturer, which may have introduced bias into the results. Another RCT found that taking a multi-species probiotic supplement from 26 to 30 weeks of pregnancy until delivery had no effect on depressive symptoms [ 49 ]. Similarly, a 2020 study showed that probiotic treatment had no effect on mental health outcomes in pregnant women [ 60 ]. The controversial findings among a handful of RCTs complicate the assessment of MTT’s potential effectiveness in treating perinatal depression. Therefore, further clinical trials are strongly suggested to reveal the potential efficacy of MTT for perinatal depressed patients. Patients with depression are at high risk for comorbidities, which often lead to ambiguity and imprecision in clinical treatment decisions [ 61 ]. To appropriately manage depression in these patients, it is crucial to enhance the understanding of MTT’s efficacy in the context of various comorbidities. In our study, MTT significantly improved depressive symptoms in patients without comorbidities or in those with coronary artery disease. However, no benefit was shown in patients with IBS, chronic diarrhea, and chronic constipation. The co-occurrence of functional gastrointestinal disorders and depression is estimated at 30% [ 62 ], and the multifactorial etiology of both conditions hinders a universal, one-strategy-fits-all treatment approach for patients with comorbid depression and gastrointestinal dysfunction [ 63 ]. This may explain the failure of MTT in treating depressed patients combined with IBS, chronic constipation, and chronic diarrhea. Notably, the administration duration is another important factor influencing the efficacy of MTT for depression. Our study supports the effectiveness of < 8 weeks and 8–12 weeks of MTT in treating depression, whereas > 12 weeks of administration was not considered effective. The administration duration of MTT in studies varied, with some lasting 4 weeks and others at least 8 weeks [ 64 ]. However, MTT administration duration for > 12 weeks has not met with special focus. This may contribute to an underestimation of the true efficacy of MTT for depression with > 12 weeks of administration duration. The limited evidence emphasizes the urgent need for more research to determine the ideal duration of MTT for achieving efficacy in terms of mental health. Several limitations may affect the results of our meta-analysis. Although we conducted detailed subgroup analyses for heterogeneity of studies, the inclusion of small studies and large diversity of gut microflora types made it necessary to be cautious in determining the overall effectiveness of MMT for depression. Besides, despite a comprehensive collection of different types of MTT to ensure a thorough assessment of their efficacy for depression, studies on FMT are still in the protocol design phase [ 65 ]. Definitive data are not available to analyze the efficacy of this emerging and promising therapy in the treatment of depression. In addition, the lack of RCTs in Africa and the fewer inclusion studies in America, Oceania and Europe led to the data being only marginally representative in terms of population-wide strategies. Finally, when combining the results of studies using different scales, although many current studies address this by combining effect sizes through SMD value [ 66 , 67 ], it has also been argued that only one effect size can be provided per study to ensure independence between effect sizes [ 68 ]. This disagreement can be further explored through the emerging 3-level meta-analysis in recent years. Conclusions Even though MTT was overall effective in the treatment of depression with acceptable safety, we remained cautious in drawing this conclusion, limited by the small sample of included studies and heterogeneity. Efficacy of MTT for depression varies by geography, patient comorbidities, and administration duration. Future trials with larger sample sizes are needed to confirm the true clinical potential of MTT for depression. documents.title: The potential effectiveness of probiotics in reducing multiple sclerosis progression in preclinical and clinical studies: A worldwide systematic review and meta-analysis.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is an immune-mediated disease characterized by nerve cell inflammation and demyelination. The effectiveness of probiotics in reducing inflammatory damage in MS. Therefore, the aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis was the potential effectiveness of probiotics in reducing Multiple Sclerosis progression in preclinical and clinical studies.
METHODS: PubMed, Scopus, Cochrane, and Google Scholar databases were searched using multiple relevant keywords, and screening was carried out based on the inclusion/exclusion criteria from January 2004 to August 16, 2024.
RESULTS: Based on our criteria, 269 papers were obtained, and after omission of unsuitable articles, 23 full-text articles consisting of 17 animal studies and six human models were selected. It was concluded that in an experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) animal model, probiotics such as Bifidobacterium, Prevotella, and Lactobacillus can decrease the T helper 1 (Th1)/Th17 ratio while inducing interferon gamma (IFN-γ) and interleukin (IL)-17 levels. In all cases, probiotics can modulate immune cells and cytokines and consequently decrease EAE signs and symptoms. In all human studies, single or multiple probiotics decreased the severity of disease and changed the gut microbiota population.
CONCLUSION: Our results showed that probiotics can control the development of MS by reducing inflammatory conditions, and may have beneficial effects in the prevention and treatment of MS.
documents.conclusions: Our results showed that probiotics can control the development of MS by reducing inflammatory conditions, and may have beneficial effects in the prevention and treatment of MS.

Introduction Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune disease characterized by autoreactive interferon gamma (IFN-γ) and interleukin (IL)-17 producing T cell-mediated inflammation, followed by neural cell demyelination [ 1 ]. Almost 2,500,000 individuals suffer from MS worldwide [ 2 ]. Although the pathogenesis of MS is multifactorial, it seems that inflammation and oxidative stress factors (OSF) are important causes of MS, and we believe that the severity of MS (according to the EDSS criteria) is directly related to the level of inflammation and OSFs [ 3 , 4 ]. Inflammation is caused by infiltration of immune cells and destruction of the myelin sheath. T and B lymphocytes can cross the blood-brain barrier (BBB), activate microglial astrocytes, and induce an inflammatory environment in which myelin is damaged and destroyed [ 5 ]. Owing to the similarity of clinical and pathophysiological features, the animal model of MS, which is called Experimental Autoimmune Encephalomyelitis (EAE), is an applicable archetype for studying the disease in non-human models [ 6 ]. EAE can be induced by immunization with myelin components and myelin protein peptides such as glycoprotein myelin oligodendrocyte (MOG) 35-55 [ 7 ]. Recently, several studies have highlighted the significance of the human microbiome in balancing and enhancing the immune system [ 8 ]. The gut-microbiota-brain axis describes a network of bidirectional communication between the gut and the CNS. This communication is crucial for regulating the homeostasis of the CNS and intestinal microbiota. Signaling through various chemical transmitters, neural mechanisms, and the immune system constitutes the communication pathways in these biological networks. The gut microbiota can influence the body through chemical communication, including both “direct” and “indirect” signals with the nervous system Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), such as butyrate, propionate, and acetate, are products of intestinal bacterial fermentation that regulate intestinal adaptive immune responses and play a vital role in CNS function. When the gut microbiome is disrupted, inflammatory cytokines and other immune cells are released, impacting the BBB and gastrointestinal permeability, as well as the levels of SCFAs and other metabolites that contribute to neuro-inflammation and demyelination [ 7 ]. Dysbiosis of the intestinal microbiota is implicated in several immune-mediated diseases, including inflammatory bowel disease, MS, type 1 diabetes, and rheumatoid arthritis [ 9 ]. Bacterial proliferation in the gut affects the immune system and can disrupt the gut barrier, resulting in an imbalance of T helper 1 (Th1)/Th2 responses, which leads to gastrointestinal autoimmune diseases [ 10 ]. Several diets have been studied in MS to modify the gut microbiome’s composition and reduce systemic inflammation, including the Swank diet, a low-fat regimen developed by Dr. R. L. Swank, and the Wahls diet, created by Dr. Terry Wahls, both of which have demonstrated beneficial effects in managing MS. Research indicates the effectiveness of probiotic-based therapies for treating MS through various mechanisms, often involving the reduction of demyelination and inflammation in the brain. It appears that greater emphasis should be placed on the significance of probiotics in the diets of these patients [ 11 ]. Probiotics can alter the gut microbiota and thus affect health status [ 11 ]. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), probiotics are living microorganisms that can improve the health benefits to the host“ [ 12 ]. In recent years, researchers have proposed probiotics as a new treatment option for autoimmune diseases [ 13 ]. Lactobacilli and bifidobacteria (predominant in the upper and lower parts of the intestine, respectively) show some therapeutic effects in experimental induced colitis, experimental inflammatory bowel disease, and experimental arthritis [ 14 , 15 ]. For example, Lactobacillus plantarum , Bifidobacterium lacti s, Lactobacillus acidophilus and Lactobacillus casei have beneficial effects in colitis, food allergies, and arthritis models. However, little is known about the exact effects of lactic acid bacteria on MS/EAE. Several studies have shown a relationship between intestinal microbiome dysbiosis and some gastrointestinal disorders in approximately 70% of MS patients [ 16 ]. Administration of probiotics or a mixture of probiotics, such as lactobacilli, streptococci, and bifidobacteria, can reduce the severity of EAE in mice, and there is evidence of the role of the gut microbiota in EAE development [ 17 , 18 ]. A recent study showed that Prevotella from the human gut suppresses EAE induction. Recently, it has been shown that changes in intestinal microbiota composition are associated with high levels of intestinal Th17 cells and enhanced disease activity in MS [ 19 ]. These findings indicate that the use of probiotics can be effective in patients with MS. There is little information regarding the effects of probiotic bacteria on the central nervous system; therefore, the aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to evaluate the potential effectiveness of probiotics on MS in preclinical and clinical studies. Methods Search strategy We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Cochran, and Google Scholar from January 2004 till 16 th August 2024, in any language. The search terms were “Probiotics” and “Multiple sclerosis” Multiple sclerosis’. The syntax written based on the MeSH database and free text methods in PubMed database are (“multiple sclerosis”[MeSH Terms] OR (“multiple”[All Fields] AND “sclerosis”[All Fields]) OR “multiple sclerosis”[All Fields] OR “encephalomyelitis, autoimmune, experimental”[MeSH Terms] OR (“encephalomyelitis”[All Fields] AND “autoimmune”[All Fields] AND “experimental”[All Fields]) OR “experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis”[All Fields] OR (“experimental”[All Fields] AND “autoimmune”[All Fields] AND “encephalomyelitis”[All Fields])) AND (“probiotic s”[All Fields] OR “probiotical”[All Fields] OR “probiotics”[MeSH Terms] OR “probiotics”[All Fields] OR “probiotic”[All Fields]). The duplicates were removed using EndNote X7 (Thomson Reuters, New York, NY, USA). The PRISMA guidelines were followed to perform this study ( S1 File ) [ 20 ]. Ethical statement This study was carried out with the Code of Ethics Committee (No. IR. KUMS. REC.1400.170) adopted by Kermanshah University of Medical Sciences and also project number 4000263. Inclusion/Exclusion criteria Animal and human studies, including those on different probiotics, have been conducted. Suitable articles were selected on the basis of certain criteria. The excluded articles were systematic reviews, meta-analyses, or narrative reviews. All studies were reviewed separately by two authors, and a third expert re-reviewed and decided on inconsistencies. Studies were included if they met all of the following criteria:1) papers using single or multiple strains of probiotics with doses of 1 × 10 8 - 3 × 10 11 CFU and 1-26 weeks’ treatment duration, 2) papers that measured the effects of probiotics on MS patients, 3) assessment of inflammation in multiple sclerosis patients, 4) papers based on the correct method, and 5) papers that included animal groups without probiotic treatment or matched control human groups. Data extraction After omission of some articles based on the criteria, the related data were extracted by two authors from an article about MS, probiotics, and the effect of probiotics, including 1) characteristics of the sample, 2) the probiotic strain used, 3) scales of effect measurement, 4) results of research, and 5) publication date. We classified data based on probiotic genus, dose of bacteria, period of treatment, examined factors, EAE Induction method, type of sample, and increase or reduction of inflammation. Risk of bias and/or quality assessment The Critical Appraisal tools of Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) were used to assess the quality (risk of bias) of each study [ 21 ]. Two reviewers independently completed the study, based on the checklist. Any inconsistencies were assessed by a third reviewer. The final quality of the studies was determined by summing the scores based on the checklist ( S1 and S2 Tables ). In addition, the SYRCLE’s risk of bias tool was used for animal studies [ 22 ] ( S3 Table ). Statistical analysis A meta-analysis was performed Using Comprehensive Meta-Analysis software (version 2.2.064) to estimate the effect of probiotics on cytokine levels, immune cell percentages, and general outcomes (clinical score or EDSS). The studies were divided into animal and human study groups, and the analysis was performed separately. Because there was significant heterogeneity between studies, the random-effects model analysis was selected for all meta-analyses. The sample sizes of the probiotic treatment and control groups, their values (mean) for each index, and their standard deviations (SDs) were used to calculate the standard differences in means (Std diff in means). The outcomes are shown as mean ±  95% confidence interval (95% CIs). Q- and I-squared statistical tests were used to calculate heterogeneity between the reports. A Q-value greater than the number of studies minus one (with a p-value lower than 0.05) was considered to indicate the existence of heterogeneity. The amount of heterogeneity is shown by an I-squared number. Due to the small number of reports, the subgroup analysis was only applicable for animal studies reporting clinical scores, in which a subgroup analysis based on the method was performed. In addition, publication bias was assessed only for the clinical score data, as it is supported by a larger body of research and offers a more robust dataset compared to other outcomes, by creating funnel plots of standard error or precision by standard difference in mean as well as using Egger’s regression test. Duval and Tweedie’s trim and fill method was used to analysis the sensitivity of the publication bias. In all analyses, a p-value of less than 0.05 was accepted as significant. Results Literature search to identify case-controlled studies According to our search keywords, 269 articles were retrieved from the databases (PubMed: 68, Scopus: 168, Cochran: 16, and Google Scholar: 17), while 124 duplicated papers, narrative reviews, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses were omitted ( Fig 1 ). The remaining 145 articles were screened and 48 articles were discussing only MS or EAE, 61 papers were only about probiotics and not their relationship with MS, seven articles were about gut microbiota and EAE, and six articles focused on the relationship between fungi and protozoa in MS, which was not our concern ( S4 Table ). Among the remaining 23 papers, 17 papers surveyed animal models, and six articles were human studies ( Table 1 ). Fig 1 Systematic literature review flow diagram. Publication bias Considering clinical score data, publication bias was assessed by drawing funnel plots and applying the Egger’s test. The both funnel plots of standard error or precision by standard difference showed asymmetric distribution of studies suggesting a potential publication bias. Also, the Egger’s test showed significant publication bias since the 1-tailed p-value (recommended by Comprehensive Meta-Analysis software) is 0.00145, and the 2-tailed p-value is 0.00290 ( Fig 8 ). Fig 8 The publication bias assessment and sensitivity analysis. The assessment of publication bias was done by drawing the funnel plots of standard error (A) or precision (B) by standard difference in mean as well as using Egger’s regression test (C). The asymmetric distribution of the studies (open circles) over the combined effect size can be observed. The sensitivity assay of publication bias was done by Duval and Tweedie’s trim and fill method which suggests that five studies are missing. These five studies are shown by solid black circles in both funnel plots of standard error (D) or precision (E). The observed and adjusted effect sizes as well as other statistical parameters of the trim and fill method are also shown (F). The Duval and Tweedie’s trim and fill method trims the asymmetric studies from the one side to locate the unbiased effect, and then fills the plot by re-inserting the trimmed studies on that side as well as their imputed counterparts to the other side of the mean effect. In the present study we chose “the right of mean” as where the missing studies should be looked for. Using these parameters, the method suggests that 5 studies are missing. Under the fixed effect model the point estimate and 95% confidence interval for the combined studies is -3.06758 (-3.36446, -2.77069). Using Trim and Fill the imputed (adjusted) point estimate is -2.40831 (-2.69064, -2.12598). Under the random effects model the point estimate and 95% confidence interval for the combined studies is -4.97506 (-6.46943, -3.48067). Using Trim and Fill the imputed point estimate is -2.51471 (-4.16838, -0.86105). The imputed studies are depicted in the funnel plots ( Fig 8 ). These results show that studies that show the reducing effect of probiotics on MS have a higher probability of being published. Discussion It seems that the innate and adaptive arms of the immune system (innate and adaptive) play an important role in the pathogenesis of MS [ 45 ]. Microglia and macrophages are professional phagocytic cells found in central nervous system (CNS) lesions in both MS and EAE models [ 46 , 47 ]. These cells are mainly responsible for the damage and removal of myelin in MS lesions [ 46 , 48 ]. In contrast, a significant proportion of CD4 + and CD8 + lymphocytes isolated from MS lesions showed an antigen-specific T cell response contributing to the disease process [ 49 ]. Th1 and Th17 cells promote inflammation of the CNS, while Th 2 and T-reg cells inhibit it [ 50 ]. In addition, the balance between pro-inflammatory Th1/Th17 cells and anti-inflammatory CD4 + FoxP3 + regulatory T cells shifts toward a pro-inflammatory response [ 51 ]. Therefore, it is possible to affect this balance, return to an anti-inflammatory response, and finally suppress the disease using potential therapeutic factors. MS and EAE are associated with the overexpression of cytokines such as IL-12, IFN-γ, IL-6, IL-1β, IL-21, and IL-23, which are partially effective in promoting the differentiation of Th1 and Th17 cells [ 52 ]. Probiotics regulate both innate and adaptive host immune response mechanisms [ 53 , 54 ]. The anti-inflammatory role of probiotics is mediated by increased levels of IL-4, transforming growth factor beta (TGF-β), IL-10 cytokines, and T-reg cells, leading to improved EAE conditions. In addition, consumption of probiotics reduces the severity of EAE by reducing Th1/Th17 levels [ 32 ]. In addition to enhancing the host immune system, probiotics have important beneficial effects in the prevention and/or management of immune-related diseases, including inflammatory bowel disease, irritable bowel syndrome, diarrhea, bacterial infections, and certain types of cancer. The development of new therapeutic strategies to improve MS pathology requires an understanding of the mechanisms of cytokine-mediated CNS damage. IFN-γ, as an important cytokine product of the Th1-type immune response, plays an important role in immune-mediated demyelination diseases such as MS because its level increases strongly during the activity of this disease [ 55 , 56 ]. In this meta-analysis, it was shown that the consumption of probiotics in patients with MS has a decreasing effect on IFN-γ levels. In other words, probiotics lead to significant clinical improvement in patients with MS. A decrease in anti-inflammatory IL-10 levels is associated with increased MS severity [ 57 ]. On the other hand, increased induction of IL-10 by Escherichia coli strain Nissle 1917-treated mice may be a preventive mechanism of inflammation and autoimmunity [ 58 , 59 ]. Accordingly, in the eight analyzed studies, the results indicated that probiotics increased IL-10 levels. MS can cause mortality, inflammation, dyslipidemia, high blood pressure, and insulin resistance. Based on our analysis of human studies, probiotic supplementation in patients with MS decreased TNF-α gene expression. In addition, probiotic supplementation significantly reduced EDSS scores (SD =  -1.839) in people with MS. Probiotics can stimulate beneficial Treg cells to maintain immune balance [ 60 ]. For example, L. plantarum WCFS1 associated with CD103 + DC shows its activity in a way that by penetrating the intestine, it increases Th2 cytokines and finally stimulates the production of Treg cells [ 61 ]. The findings shown in Fig 6 indicate that consumption of probiotics can stimulate Treg cells. Finally, IL-17, an inflammatory marker in MS, has been shown to decrease with the administration of probiotics (mono-strain in 8 studies and a mixture of probiotics in 4 animal studies). However, it has only been examined in one human study, which does not demonstrate a significant effect on its level [ 27 – 38 , 41 , 45 ]. Conversely, IL-10, an inhibitory cytokine that is reduced in MS patients, increased with the administration of probiotics in 10 animal studies (monostrain in 6 and mixture in 4 studies) and 2 human studies, which may help improve MS symptoms [ 26 , 29 – 32 , 34 , 35 , 37 , 38 , 41 , 43 , 45 ]. Additionally, IFN-γ decreased in 10 animal studies (6 with probiotic alone and 4 with probiotics in combination) and one human study [ 26 , 28 , 30 , 31 , 33 – 35 , 37 , 38 , 41 , 45 ], while it increased in 3 animal studies [ 29 , 32 , 36 ]. Regarding TNF-α, no increase was observed in the animal model with the administration of probiotics, but a decrease in this inflammatory cytokine was reported in 4 studies [ 26 , 30 , 37 , 41 ]. In human studies, it was increased in one case and decreased in another [ 43 , 45 ]. Conclusion Twenty-seven animal and seven human studies systematically demonstrated the effects of probiotic consumption on MS. These findings indicate that probiotic consumption may have potentially beneficial effects in reducing the incidence and severity of MS and in delaying disease progression. Since probiotic therapy may be considered a promising opportunity for the treatment of MS, physicians and nutritionists should consider approved probiotic supplements to manage health concerns in MS. documents.title: Comparative study for fatigue prevalence in subjects with diseases: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
documents.abstract: Fatigue is one of the common symptoms in individuals with diseases or disorders, significantly affecting quality of life (QoL) and the prognosis of diseases. This study aimed to comprehensively compare the features of fatigue across a wide range of diseases. We systematically searched the PubMed and Cochrane Library databases from inception to March 31st, 2021, and conducted a meta-analysis to generate precise estimates. The analyses were stratified by classification of diseases, gender, and severity of fatigue (moderate and severe), and study quality was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS). In total, 214 articles (233 prevalence data) met our eligibility criteria, covering 102,024 participants (mean 438 ± 1,421) across 88 diseases. Among these, seventy-eight data sets (52,082 participants) and thirty-nine data sets (10,389 participants) reported gender- and severity-related fatigue prevalence. The overall prevalence among subjects with 88 diseases was 49.4% [95% CI 46.9-52.1]. According to the International Classification of Diseases-10 (ICD-10) classification, the highest prevalence of fatigue (65.9% [95% CI 54.9-79.6]) was observed in patients with mental/behavioral diseases, whereas the lowest prevalence (34.7% [95% CI 24.5-49.2]) was found among those with circulatory system diseases. A slight female dominance (43.5% vs. 49.8%) was observed in the total data, with the most notable female predominance (1.8-fold) seen in patients with low back pain. The top disease groups with a moderate to severe level of fatigue included gastroparesis (92.3%), pulmonary hypertension (90.0%), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD, 83.2%), and multiple sclerosis (80.0%). These results are the first to comprehensively show the comparative features of fatigue prevalence among subjects across 88 diseases. Our findings provide valuable reference data for future research on fatigue and for the management of patients with fatigue.Prospero registration number: CRD42021270494.

Introduction Fatigue is one of the most frequent complaints not only among subjects with diseases, like 50% of cancer patients 1 , but also in the general population, approximately 16% 2 . Short-term fatigue can be a predictable physiological response to intense activity and typically does not affect daily life 3 . However, pathological fatigue, especially when chronic and uncontrolled, leads to a poor quality of life (QoL) and impairs daily efficiency 4 , 5 . Many factors affect the prevalence of fatigue, including age, sex, ethnicity, occupation, and psychological condition 5 – 8 . For example, females are known to be more susceptible to cancer-related fatigue (CRF), with a prevalence about 2.1 times higher than that of males 9 . Health-related factors such as sleep quality, obesity, nutritional status, stress, and illness further influence the frequency and severity of fatigue 10 – 12 . Among these, the presence of a disorder or disease is the primary determinants of the prevalence and severity of fatigue; for instance, approximately 70% and 82% of individuals with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and fibromyalgia, respectively, experience fatigue 13 , 14 . Additionally, other disease-related factors, such as malnutrition in patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), also affect prevalence of fatigue 15 . Disease-related fatigue is not only a primary symptom of many disorders but also a factor that influences the clinical course of the disease, including its outcomes. Increased fatigue has been associated with the progression of dialysis initiation in patients with chronic kidney disease 16 , and with increased mortality in individuals with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) 17 . Moreover, fatigue has been linked to the prognosis of diseases, with potentially higher recurrence rates of stroke and breast cancer among patients reporting more frequent or severe fatigue 18 , 19 . Therefore, assessing the presence and severity of fatigue is important in the management of patients, particularly those with chronic illnesses 20 , 21 . To date, although numerous studies have examined the prevalence of fatigue in individuals with specific diseases, there is a lack of research comparing the prevalence and severity of fatigue across a diverse range of conditions. Therefore, this study aims to conduct a comprehensive comparison of fatigue prevalence and its clinical features across various diseases. Methods Study design To investigate the prevalence of fatigue in subjects with various diseases worldwide, research papers containing data on fatigue prevalence in diseased individuals were systematically reviewed and analyzed. This systematic review has been registered in the PROSPERO database (CRD42021270490) and was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Data sources and keywords Data were collected from two databases (PubMed and the Cochrane Library) and searches were conducted for publications available through March 31st, 2021. The search keywords included ‘fatigue’ [MeSH term] and 'prevalence.' The search terms used were "Fatigue [Title] AND Prevalence [Title/Abstract]" OR "Fatigue [Title] AND Frequency [Title/Abstract]" in both PubMed and the Cochrane Library. All languages were included. Eligibility criteria Studies were screened using the following inclusion criteria: (1) studies including patients diagnosed with a specific disease in International Classification of Diseases-10 (ICD-10), (2) studies reporting fatigue prevalence from cross-sectional or longitudinal designs, (3) studies with fatigue prevalence data obtained through fatigue-specific assessment tools or physician interviews. The exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) studies reporting lifetime prevalence of fatigue, (2) studies focusing on a specific fatigue subdomain, such as only physical or mental, (3) studies on fatigue induction after specific medical procedures, (4) studies on myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) prevalence, (5) studies in patients with cancer, (6) studies with fewer than 30 participants, (7) review articles, (8) duplicate articles, and (9) articles without full texts. All languages were included. Review process and data extraction Initially, three authors (NHP, EUK, JHY) searched and screened all titles and abstracts retrieved. The full texts of eligible studies were then independently reviewed and cross-checked by these authors. In the event of disagreement, discussions were held among the authors, with the final decision made by the corresponding author (Professor Son CG). Data extracted from each study included the first author’s name, study title, study type (cross-sectional, longitudinal), number of participants (total, male, female), classification of diseases (by ICD-10), diagnosed disease, fatigue prevalence, severity levels of fatigue (moderate, severe), fatigue diagnostic method (questionnaire, interview), fatigue assessment tools, publication year, and the continent/country where the study was conducted. Data coding and synthesis Regarding the longitudinal study, only the first observed data were selected. We synthesized the fatigue prevalence without differentiation of ‘chronic’, ‘general’ or ‘severe’ fatigue. On the other hand, we produced the severity-related data using only studies presenting simultaneously ‘moderate’ and ‘severe’ fatigue prevalence (each exclusively) and synthesized ‘moderate to severe’ prevalence by combining these. If a study contained three levels of fatigue—‘mild or no,’ ‘moderate,’ ‘severe’—fatigue data. we excluded data on ‘mild or no’ fatigue. Diseases were classified according to organ systems or ICD-10 into 12 categories: nervous system, musculoskeletal system, infectious diseases, immune system, digestive system, genitourinary system, respiratory system, circulatory system, endocrine/metabolic system, transplantation, mental/behavioral diseases, and others. Study quality assessment The quality of each included article was independently assessed by two investigators using the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale (NOS) adapted for cross-sectional and cohort studies. The assessment of each article’s quality was based on three categories: participant selection, comparability of study controls, and appropriateness of outcome. A NOS scores were categorized as high (> 7), moderate (5–7), or low (< 5). Any discrepancies in scoring were resolved through discussions among the four investigators. Meta-analysis We conducted a meta-analysis to calculate the mean prevalence and 95% confidence intervals (95% CI). To improve statistical analysis, the prevalence from each study was log-transformed, and the pooled estimates were then converted back to the original prevalence scale. Additionally, the prevalence of fatigue without transformation was also analyzed to test the robustness of the results. To explain the potentially high interstudy heterogeneity, the pooled outcome measures and their corresponding 95% CI were calculated using a random-effects model fitted with the restricted maximum likelihood estimator. The I 2 statistic was also used to evaluate the degree of heterogeneity between studies. All analyses were performed using the “meta” package (by Guido Schwarzer) in R version 4.2.1. Statistical significance was determined using hypothesis testing to analyze differences between the groups. In all analyses, meta-regression was applied, and p-values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant. Result Characteristics of the included studies Of the 3,152 articles initially screened in PubMed and Cochrane, 214 articles (233 sets of prevalence data) met our eligibility criteria. These comprised 175 cross-sectional studies (193 data) and 39 longitudinal studies (40 data) (Fig. 1 ). In total, 102,024 participants (438 ± 1,421 participants) with 88 different types of individual diseases were enrolled. Of these, data for 78 sets (involving 52,082 participants, with 21,079 males and 31,003 females) included gender information (Table 1 , Fig. 2 ). According to the study quality assessment using the NOS scale, 85.0% (182 out of 214 articles) scored 5 or higher, indicating that their study quality is at least medium. Fig. 1 Flow diagram. Using total 233 data, the meta-analyzed data for the overall prevalence and their 95% confidence intervals (95% CI) are presented according to international classification of diseases-10 (ICD-10). Thirty-eight articles (39 data, with 10,389 participants) reported information on fatigue severity (‘moderate’ and ‘severe’). The major studies (214 data) assessed the prevalence of fatigue (including its severity) using 28 types of self-reported, questionnaire-based measurement tools. These included the Fatigue Severity Scale (FSS, 59 data), Chalder Fatigue Questionnaire (CFQ, 18 data), Checklist Individual Strength (CIS, 18 data), Fatigue Impact Scale (FIS, 14 data), Fatigue Assessment Scale (FAS, 11 data), and Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory (MFI, 10 data), among others. Approximately 71% of the studies (165 data) were conducted since 2011, with 74% of the studies originating from Europe (126 data) and North America (47 data) respectively (Table 1 ). Comparison of fatigue prevalence by organ-system An overall prevalence of 102,024 participants (233 data for 88 individual diseases) was 49.4% [95% CI 46.9 -52.1] (Fig. 2 , Table 2 ). According to the International Classification of Diseases-10 (ICD-10), patients with mental/behavioral diseases reported the highest fatigue prevalence at 65.9% [95% CI 54.5–79.6], followed by those with transplantation (56.8% [95% CI 42.7–75.5]) and with diseases of the respiratory system (56.3% [95% CI 43.8–72.5]). Meanwhile patients diseases in circulatory system showed the lowest fatigue prevalence at 34.7% [95% CI 24.5–49.2), respectively (Fig. 2 ). Comparison of fatigue prevalence by individual disease Regarding fatigue associated with 88 individual diseases (total 102,024 participants), subjects with five diseases showed a fatigue prevalence of over 90%; osteogenesis imperfecta (96.4% [95% CI: 73.9–100]), whiplash-associated disorders (93.8% [95% CI: 65.6–100]), postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS, 93.6% [95% CI: 69.7–100]), gastroparesis (92.3% [95% CI: 78.4–100]), and pulmonary hypertension (90.0% [95% CI: 74.5–100]). In contrast, the lowest prevalence was observed in patients with Lyme disease (9.0% [95% CI: 4.7–17.3]). Among diseases with the three largest participant numbers (over 10,000 subjects), patients with multiple sclerosis (20 data, 14,480 subjects) had a fatigue prevalence of 60.2% [95% CI 55.1–65.6], while patients with HIV infection (11 data, 16,147 subjects) and heart failure (3 data, 12,715 subjects) presented relatively low prevalence of 38.2% [95% CI: 24.7–58.9] and 38.3% [95% CI: 28.0–52.5], respectively (Table 2 ). The differences in fatigue prevalence related to individual diseases were statistically significant (p < 0.001). Comparison of fatigue prevalence by gender Among 52,082 participants (21,079 males and 31,003 females) provided with gender information, 73 data for 29 diseases (51,676 participants: 20,869 males and 30,807 females) met our criteria (existence of gender-specific information for ≥ 100 participants) for gender-related analysis. The total fatigue prevalence was female-dominant at a ratio of 1.15-fold, with rates of 43.8% [95% CI: 39.3–48.8] for males and 50.3% [95% CI: 46.1–54.9] for females. Subjects with 23 diseases (79.3%) exhibited a female-dominant pattern, most notably in patients with chronic low back pain (1.77-fold), giardiasis (1.60-fold), spinal cord injury (1.60-fold), and EBV infection (1.50-fold). Conversely, psoriatic arthritis demonstrated the most male-dominant fatigue prevalence pattern at 0.68-fold (based on one RCT) (Fig. 3 ). Fig. 3 Gender-related fatigue prevalence rate. Using only 73 data containing sex-related fatigue information, the meta-analyzed prevalence and their 95% confidence intervals (95% CI) are presented for both male and female according to each disease. Comparison of fatigue prevalence by severity Thirty-nine data (10,389 participants) reported prevalence rate by severity information (moderate versus severe exclusively) for 28 individual diseases. The overall fatigue prevalence was 55.3% [95% CI; 49.6–61.6], while the fatigue severity ratio of ‘severe’ to ‘moderate’ was 0.87, respectively. Patients suffering from Pompe disease (6.1-folds), epilepsy (2.8-folds), pulmonary hypertension (2.0-folds) and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE, 2.0-folds) reported over 2-folds ‘severe’ to ‘moderate’ ratio, respectively (Fig. 4 ). Discussion From 214 articles reporting 233 data across 88 individual diseases (involving 102,024 participants) in 44 countries, we herein systematically produced the characteristics of fatigue prevalence among diseased subjects worldwide. The pooled prevalence rate of fatigue was 48.6% (data not shown), which is nearly the same as that found in meta-analysis data (49.4% [95% CI 46.9–52.1]) (Fig. 2 , Table 2 ). These results suggest that approximately half of patients with illnesses experience clinically significant fatigue. This prevalence rate is nearly three times higher than the 16.4% (95% CI, 13.6–19.9) observed in the general population of 623,624 individuals 2 . Among disease-related fatigue, CRF is most well-known. Two recent systematic reviews reported CRF prevalence rates of 49.0% and 52.0% 22 , 23 , which are nearly the same as our current data across 88 types of diseases. In our current results, patients with mental or behavioral disorders showed the highest prevalence of fatigue at 65.9% [95% CI 54.5–79.6] (Fig. 2 ), with rates derived from patients suffering from functional movement disorders (71.7%), major depressive disorder (MDD, 64.7%), and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD, 61.8%), respectively (Table 2 ). These three disorders belonged in psychiatric problems, which originate from brain. Structural and functional changes in the brain are known to be an important contributor to development of notable fatigue, such as 93.6% in patients with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS), 73.3% in brain injury and 69.9% in chronic headache (Table 2 ). In addition, patients with multiple sclerosis (14,480 participants) and Parkinson’s disease (2,521 participant) presented 60.2% and 54.3% of fatigue prevalence, as already known as diseases leading to high rates of fatigue 24 , 25 . Long COVID has gained attention due to its overlap with many clinical features of ME/CFS, a well-known complex, multisystem neuroimmune disease 26 , 27 . In our data, 47.9% of subjects with COVID-19 infection reported fatigue (Table 2 ). The brain-related prominent fatigue symptom was evident in our previous CRF data, showing the highest prevalence (52.5%) among patients with brain tumors compared to eight other cancer types 1 . Among 88 different diseases, patients with five conditions showed a fatigue prevalence exceeding 90%. The highest prevalence was observed in osteogenesis imperfecta (96.4%), followed by whiplash-associated disorders (93.8%), POTS (93.6%), gastroparesis (92.3%), and pulmonary hypertension (90.0%), respectively (Table 2 ). Osteogenesis imperfecta is a common hereditary connective tissue disorder characterized by extremely fragile bones and pain, with a prevalence of approximately 90% 28 . Fatigue is often recognized as a cluster of symptoms that accompany other issues, such as pain, depression, anxiety, or sleep disturbances. In particular, fatigue and pain mutually influence each other, and these symptoms often co-occur in connective tissue disorders 29 , 30 . Both fibromyalgia and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) are typical pain-presenting connective tissue diseases, while they showed high fatigue prevalence rates as 82.2% and 63.4% (Table 2 ). Regarding Whiplash-associated disorders (93.8% prevalence of fatigue) and gastroparesis (92.3% prevalence of fatigue), both conditions are typically associated with severe pain and a tendency for dysfunction without identifiable lesions or structural pathology in the majority of affected individuals 31 , 32 . One cohort study reported that among 3,230 individuals with fatigue, approximately 65% (1,967 subjects) had a co-symptom of pain, depression, or both of them 33 . Another study reported that the presence particularly of fatigue affected both the physical and mental aspects of health-related QoL, contrast to pain affecting physical-dominant QoL 34 . In our present meta-analyses, some data were calculated from a relatively small number of studies or participants, with an average of 438 ± 1,421 individuals (Table 1 ). However, data derived from sixteen diseases enrolled over 1,000 participants, including subjects with HIV infection (16,147 participants), multiple sclerosis (14,480 participants), heart failure (12,715 participants), rheumatoid arthritis (8,251 participants), and primary immunodeficiency (2,366 participants), respectively (Table 2 ). Individuals with primary immunodeficiency (18.2%) or acquired immunodeficiency (HIV infection, 38.2%) showed relatively low fatigue prevalence. Additionally, patients with heart failure had a 38.3% prevalence of fatigue, which is inconsistent with its impact on health-related status (Table 2 ). These observations suggest that disease-related fatigue may depend more on the presence of specific conditions than on the overall severity of the disease 35 . An analysis from 1,696 patients with chronic diseases revealed that fatigue severity was notably influenced by pain, sleep disturbance, and physical dysfunction, and female sex 36 . In fact, pain is not the primary symptom for most individuals with primary or acquired immunodeficiency without advanced complications, as well as those with heart failure 37 , 38 . On the other hand, fatigue prevalence is affected by many factors, including gender, obesity, age, ethnicity, occupation, sleep quality, and psychological condition 5 – 8 , 12 . Our data showed the high frequent rate of fatigue (59.1%) in subjects with obesity (Table 2 ). Other groups have indicated obesity as a contributor to fatigue in the general population as well as in diseased subjects such as those post-stroke and even in ME/CFS 39 – 41 . Females are generally more prone to fatigue than males, with our previous studies indicating a 1.5-fold increase 2 , 42 . Most data from our studies on 29 different diseases showed a female-dominant or equivalent pattern of fatigue prevalence, with a few exceptions (Fig. 3 ). Among the studies included in our analysis, subjects with low back pain showed the most female-predominant fatigue (1.8-fold, 17.3% vs. 30.7%) 43 , while subjects with psoriatic arthritis presented a male-predominant fatigue rate (0.7-fold, 40.9% vs. 27.7%), respectively 44 . However, we must exercise caution or acknowledge limitations regarding the male-dominant fatigue prevalence in subjects with psoriatic arthritis, because another recent study presented reverse data 45 . The medical impact of fatigue relies on its severity and/or duration. Therefore, the guidelines for the management of fatigue recommend assessing the severity of fatigue, not just the presence of fatigue 35 . In general, the medical concern focuses on the moderate to severe level of fatigue in the clinical field 46 . When we analyzed data from 39 studies (10,389 participants across 28 diseases) containing information on the prevalence of severity-informed fatigue, the total prevalence rate of ‘moderate to severe’ fatigue was 55.3% [95% CI 49.6–61.6] (Table 2 ). The top 4 diseases showed over 80% prevalence of ‘moderate to severe’ level of fatigue, such as gastroparesis (92.3%), pulmonary hypertension (90.0%), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD, 83.2%) and multiple sclerosis (80.0%). Meanwhile the highest prevalence of severe fatigue (67.1%) was observed in individuals with Pompe disease (Fig. 4 ). Prominent fatigue has been well recognized as an important feature of late-onset Pompe disease, which shows progressive weakness in the heart and skeletal muscles, caused by mutations in a gene responsible for breaking down glycogen 47 . The second-highest rate of severe fatigue, found in 60.0% of patients with pulmonary hypertension, is likely related to the core symptom of dyspnea, given that pulmonary hypertension is a potentially fatal disease 48 . We herein analyzed the overall comparison of fatigue prevalence in subjects with diseases or disorders. However, our study has some limitations such as the small number of studies and participants in certain diseases, and the lack of data on risk factors for fatigue and fatigue severity. The disease-related fatigue can also be influenced by the stage of the disease and therapeutic interventions. The CRF prevalence varies significantly depending on the treatment phase, with ‘moderate to severe’ fatigue reported in 30.8% of patients before treatment compared to 46.1% during treatment. This variation is why we excluded CRF prevalence data from the present study. Additionally, we found that the prevalence of fatigue in inflammatory bowel disease increased 1.7-fold during the ‘active phase’ compared to the ‘remission phase’ 49 . Another issue is the applications of different fatigue-assessment tools and inconsistent cut-off for prevalence and severity of fatigue in each study. Accordingly, we require to consider the carefulness in interpretations of the present data related to these limitations. There is no established standard treatment for chronic, severe fatigue associated with specific diseases 50 . Moreover, physicians often underestimate the importance of fatigue, creating barriers to effective communication about this symptom. For example, one study reported that approximately 66% of cancer patients had never discussed their fatigue with their doctor 51 . Fatigue, particularly during treatment, is associated with reduced treatment compliance 52 . Given the limitations of using medications to manage fatigue, non-pharmacological treatments are increasingly recommended 53 . Therefore, we emphasize the need for clearer assessment and differentiation of fatigue characteristics among patients with diseased conditions. Our current data provide a comparative reference for healthcare providers to make patient-specific decisions on fatigue management. Conclusion The present results represent the first comprehensive showcase of the comparative features of fatigue prevalence and severity among subjects with 88 different diseases. Our findings indicate that approximately half of the patients suffering from an illness report clinically significant fatigue, with a prevalence rate of 49.4% [95% CI 46.9–52.1], along with a slight female dominance (43.5% vs. 49.8%), but a notable female predominance (1.8-fold) in patients with low back pain. According to the ICD-10 classification, fatigue prevalence rates were highest in patients with mental/behavioral diseases (65.9% [95% CI 54.9–79.6]) and lowest among those with circulatory system diseases (34.7% [95% CI 24.5–49.2]). The top disease groups exhibiting moderate to severe levels of fatigue included gastroparesis (92.3%), pulmonary hypertension (90.0%), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD, 83.2%), and multiple sclerosis (80.0%). Our findings offer valuable reference data for future research on fatigue and for the management of patients experiencing fatigue. Supplementary Information Supplementary Information. documents.title: Effect of probiotics and paraprobiotics on patients with sleep disorders and sub-healthy sleep conditions: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The microbial-gut-brain axis has received much attention in recent years, and regulating intestinal flora can effectively improve sleep disorders, which hints the potential effects of probiotics on sleep disorders, but lack of research evidence for meta-analysis. Therefore, this study aims to quantitatively evaluate the influence of probiotics on sleep disorders and sub-healthy sleep conditions.
METHODS: Up to 2023, online databases including Pubmed, Embase, Cochrane library, Web of science have been searched for studies involving adults who consume probiotics or paraprobiotics in controlled trials, during which, changes in subjective and/or objective sleep parameters and contributing factors in sleeping quality are examined. We conduct a meta-analysis of 11 clinical randomized controlled studies.
RESULTS: Probiotic supplementation improves sleep states to some extent in adults with sleep disorders and healthy adults with condition-induced sleep disorders (-0.34 [-0.56 to -0.13]; I 2 = 42.6%; p = 0.001). Meanwhile, subgroup analysis shows that the effect of probiotics on improving sleep disorders is influenced by other factors such as the health states of the subjects, the duration of the intervention, the type of strain, and the test criteria.
CONCLUSION: Probiotics and paraprobiotics have a significant positive effect on the sleep quality of adults with sleep disorders or sub-healthy sleep conditions. However, the therapeutic effects of probiotics on sleep problems need future additional trials.
SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://inplasy.com/inplasy-2022-12-0066/, identifier 2022120066.
